Introduction

A messenger has just obtained a message at a station sss of a directed network. A pursuer occupies another station, and both positions are visible. They move alternately, the messenger first, using one directed connection or waiting. The messenger wants to deliver to a designated recipient ttt before interception. Receipt completes the task immediately, even if the pursuer is at ttt: the pursuer can intercept the messenger but cannot disable the recipient.

A direct connection s→ts\to ts→t makes delivery immediate. We study the additional communication supported by the network: source–recipient pairs without a direct connection for which delivery is nevertheless guaranteed against every allowed initial pursuer position. Write I(G)I(G)I(G) for their number. The three extremal quantities are

MV(n)=max⁡∣V(G)∣=nI(G),ME(m)=max⁡∣E(G)∣=mI(G),M(n,m)=max⁡∣V(G)∣=n, ∣E(G)∣=mI(G). M_V(n)=\max_{|V(G)|=n} I(G),\qquad M_E(m)=\max_{|E(G)|=m} I(G),\qquad M(n,m)=\max_{|V(G)|=n,\ |E(G)|=m} I(G). MV​(n)=∣V(G)∣=nmax​I(G),ME​(m)=∣E(G)∣=mmax​I(G),M(n,m)=∣V(G)∣=n, ∣E(G)∣=mmax​I(G).

Isolated vertices are allowed. Removing them preserves III, so the arc-only maximum is finite: a graph with m>0m>0m>0 arcs has at most 2m2m2m nonisolated vertices.

The original problem and a layered subset construction arose in Alexandra Ignatova’s 2023 project, mentored by Angel Raychev. A public 2023 abstract records that provenance (Ignatova 2023); the retained manuscript is dated February 2024 (Ignatova 2024). Ignatova and Raychev had already established the upper bound I(G)≤n(n−3)I(G)\le n(n-3)I(G)≤n(n−3) and investigated two-in/two-out-regular constructions. This account reconstructs that bound, distinguishes the original construction from its corrected analysis, and supplies new attaining families among the September 2026 extensions. The full extremal classification remains open.

The general arguments are ordinary mathematical proofs. The accompanying Lean development formalizes the actual alternating game, a certificate-to-strategy theorem, safe branching, camping obstructions, a complete universally winning 12-vertex example, complementary-block two-move delivery, and the numerical staircase deduction from explicit counting hypotheses. The graph-to-counting bridge and existence of attaining blocks remain ordinary arguments. It does not claim to formalize all the general extremal theorems.

The game and its elementary structure

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite loopless digraph. Opposite arcs are allowed. A legal move from xxx goes to xxx or to an outgoing neighbor; write C(x)={x}∪N+(x).C(x)=\{x\}\cup N^+(x).C(x)={x}∪N+(x). Fix s,t∈Vs,t\in Vs,t∈V and c≠sc\ne sc=s. If s=ts=ts=t, receipt has already occurred. Otherwise the messenger moves first. On its turn it chooses v∈C(s)v\in C(s)v∈C(s). If v=tv=tv=t, delivery wins immediately. If v≠tv\ne tv=t and v=cv=cv=c, it is captured. Otherwise the pursuer chooses c′∈C(c)c'\in C(c)c′∈C(c); equality c′=vc'=vc′=v is capture. The process repeats. Infinite play without delivery is a messenger loss.

Let WG(s,t)W_G(s,t)WG​(s,t) mean that, for every initial c≠sc\ne sc=s, there exists a messenger strategy guaranteeing delivery against every pursuer strategy. The messenger observes ccc; its strategy may depend on it. Then I(G)=#{(s,t):s≠t, (s,t)∉E, WG(s,t)}. I(G)=\#\{(s,t):s\ne t,\ (s,t)\notin E,\ W_G(s,t)\}. I(G)=#{(s,t):s=t, (s,t)∈/E, WG​(s,t)}. If w(G)w(G)w(G) counts all guaranteed pairs including the diagonal, then exactly w(G)=n+m+I(G).w(G)=n+m+I(G).w(G)=n+m+I(G).

The terminal rule matters. In the directed diamond s→a→ts\to a\to ts→a→t, s→b→ts\to b\to ts→b→t, the messenger chooses the intermediate vertex not occupied by the pursuer and delivers on its next turn. But reaching a vertex that would be safe as a recipient does not justify using it as an intermediate stop. The pursuer gets an intervening move before the message can be forwarded again.

Camping obstructions

Lemma 1 (source domination). If c≠sc\ne sc=s and N+(s)⊆C(c)N^+(s)\subseteq C(c)N+(s)⊆C(c), there is no guaranteed indirect pair with source sss.

Proof. The pursuer starts at ccc and waits while the messenger waits. Every nonterminal departure from sss is either an immediate collision or is captured on the following pursuer turn. Waiting forever is not delivery. □\square□

Lemma 2 (predecessor domination). Put Dt=N−(t)D_t=N^-(t)Dt​=N−(t). If Dt⊆C(c)D_t\subseteq C(c)Dt​⊆C(c), an indirect guaranteed source for ttt must equal ccc.

Proof. For any other source the pursuer may start at ccc. Every indirect delivery must first enter DtD_tDt​, where the pursuer can capture before the next messenger turn. □\square□

In particular, a source counted by III has outdegree at least two, and a recipient counted by III has indegree at least two. An indegree-one recipient is blocked by its unique predecessor. In an undirected network, interpreted as two opposite arcs per edge, the pursuer can start at ttt and catch the messenger upon its first arrival at a neighbor of ttt. Thus I=0I=0I=0 for every such network.

The two degree conditions are necessary, not sufficient. Neither the absence of a one-vertex directed separator nor the existence of two internally disjoint routes characterizes this game. Adding a→ba\to ba→b to the diamond destroys its only indirect guarantee, although both routes remain. Consequently III is not monotone under adding arcs.

Lemma 3 (two-move criterion). For an indirect pair (s,t)(s,t)(s,t), put B=N+(s)∩N−(t)B=N^+(s)\cap N^-(t)B=N+(s)∩N−(t). Delivery is guaranteed within two messenger moves exactly when for every c≠s,B⊈C(c).\text{for every }c\ne s,\qquad B\not\subseteq C(c).for every c=s,B⊆C(c).

Proof. Choose an intermediate vertex of B∖C(c)B\setminus C(c)B∖C(c), survive every pursuer response, and deliver. Conversely, any successful two-move indirect delivery must use such an intermediate. Waiting on the first move cannot reach a nonadjacent recipient on the second. □\square□

Components, zero minima, and the vertex bound

Removing isolated vertices preserves III. More generally, I(G⊔H)=I(G)+I(H).I(G\sqcup H)=I(G)+I(H).I(G⊔H)=I(G)+I(H). There are no cross-component routes; a pursuer in the other component cannot interfere with a route in the messenger’s component.

Proposition 4. At every admissible (n,m)(n,m)(n,m) the minimum of III is zero.

Proof. For n≥2n\ge2n≥2, list all nonloop arcs row by row and retain the first mmm. There are full outgoing rows, at most one partial row, and empty rows. Full rows have only direct recipients; empty rows cannot move. If a full row exists, its vertex blocks every indirect attempt from the partial row by Lemma 1. Otherwise successors of the partial row have no outgoing arcs, so no indirect route exists. The empty and one-vertex cases are immediate. □\square□

Theorem 5 (original upper bound). For every n≥3n\ge3n≥3, I(G)≤n(n−3).I(G)\le n(n-3).I(G)≤n(n−3).

Proof. A recipient of indegree zero or one has no indirect guaranteed sources. A recipient of indegree d≥2d\ge2d≥2 has at most n−1−d≤n−3n-1-d\le n-3n−1−d≤n−3, after excluding itself and its direct predecessors. Sum over recipients. □\square□

For n≥4n\ge4n≥4, equality forces every recipient to have indegree two and every missing pair to be guaranteed. Every source must then have outdegree at least two; the degree sum forces outdegree exactly two. Conversely, a two-in/two-out-regular graph with every pair guaranteed attains equality. Thus attaining the vertex bound is exactly a sparse universal-delivery construction problem.

Sharp arc-budget upper bounds

Let AAA be the vertices of outdegree at least two and BBB those of indegree at least two. Write q=∣A∣q=|A|q=∣A∣, r=∣B∣r=|B|r=∣B∣, b=∣A∩B∣b=|A\cap B|b=∣A∩B∣, and let e(A,B)e(A,B)e(A,B) count arcs from AAA to BBB. Every counted pair belongs to A×BA\times BA×B, and direct and diagonal pairs are excluded. Hence I(G)≤qr−b−e(A,B),e(A,B)≥max⁡{0,2q+2r−m}.(1) I(G)\le qr-b-e(A,B),\qquad e(A,B)\ge\max\{0,2q+2r-m\}. \tag{1} I(G)≤qr−b−e(A,B),e(A,B)≥max{0,2q+2r−m}.(1) The second inequality follows by adding the total outgoing degree in AAA and incoming degree in BBB: each arc is counted at most once except those in A×BA\times BA×B.

We also need two elementary obstructions. If xxx has indegree zero and x→tx\to tx→t with ttt of indegree two, then ttt has no indirect guaranteed sources. Its other predecessor blocks every indirect route: a route from elsewhere cannot reach xxx, while x→tx\to tx→t itself is direct. Dually, if ttt is a sink, x→tx\to tx→t, and xxx has outdegree two, then xxx has no indirect guaranteed recipients. Its other successor blocks every potentially successful indirect departure. This dual argument is proved directly and does not assume invariance under reversing the graph.

Equality structure

Theorem 8. For k≥6k\ge6k≥6, equality in Theorem 6 holds exactly when deleting isolated vertices leaves a two-in/two-out-regular graph on kkk vertices with every pair guaranteed.

Proof. The numerical bounds away from the three corners are strict. In the (k−1,k)(k-1,k)(k−1,k) corner, a member of A∖BA\setminus BA∖B gives the strict zero-column estimate above; if A⊆BA\subseteq BA⊆B, then b=k−1b=k-1b=k−1 gives a strict bound directly. The other corner is analogous. In the (k,k)(k,k)(k,k) corner, A≠BA\ne BA=B gives the strict bound (k−2)2(k-2)^2(k−2)2. Hence A=BA=BA=B, all 2k2k2k arcs lie on these kkk vertices, and all incoming and outgoing degrees equal two. Equality then says that every eligible missing pair is guaranteed. □\square□

Theorem 9. For k≥6k\ge6k≥6, equality in Theorem 7 holds exactly for graphs whose nonisolated support has the following properties: it has k+1k+1k+1 vertices; one vertex uuu has outdegree one and indegree two; a different vertex vvv has indegree one and outdegree two; all other degrees are two; u→vu\to vu→v is absent; and every missing nonloop pair with source of outdegree two and recipient of indegree two is guaranteed.

Proof. Strengthening the strict inequalities in Theorem 7 excludes all cases except q=r=kq=r=kq=r=k and b=k−1b=k-1b=k−1. In the corner (q,r)=(k−1,k)(q,r)=(k-1,k)(q,r)=(k−1,k), values b≥2b\ge2b≥2 are strict directly. If b≤1b\le1b≤1, at least k−2k-2k−2 members of AAA lie outside BBB, and at most one has positive indegree. The zero-column argument gives I≤k2−4k+6<k(k−3)+2I\le k^2-4k+6<k(k-3)+2I≤k2−4k+6<k(k−3)+2. The dual corner uses the zero-row argument. In the remaining (k,k)(k,k)(k,k) corner, for b=2b=2b=2 at least three indegree-zero sources give two zero columns; for 3≤b≤k−23\le b\le k-23≤b≤k−2 the one-column argument retains at least two diagonal exclusions. The other excluded cases already have strict bounds for k≥6k\ge6k≥6.

Write A∖B={v}A\setminus B=\{v\}A∖B={v} and B∖A={u}B\setminus A=\{u\}B∖A={u}. Equality forces e(A,B)=2k−1e(A,B)=2k-1e(A,B)=2k−1. The outgoing degree sum in AAA and incoming degree sum in BBB are each at least 2k2k2k, while their sum is at most m+e(A,B)=4km+e(A,B)=4km+e(A,B)=4k. Thus all these degrees equal two. Exactly one arc starts outside AAA and one ends outside BBB, and they are distinct. Vertex vvv cannot have indegree zero: it would give a zero column containing at least k−3>0k-3>0k−3>0 eligible missing pairs. Hence it receives the unique arc ending outside BBB. Dually uuu emits the unique arc starting outside AAA. Every vertex outside A∪BA\cup BA∪B is isolated, and the two exceptional arcs being distinct implies that u→vu\to vu→v is absent. Adding the missing arc u→vu\to vu→v in Theorem 9 gives a two-regular digraph. It is not asserted that this completed graph is automatically universally winning.

Sparse constructions with a linear deficit

A safe branching principle

Lemma 10. Suppose distinct vertices have closed move sets intersecting in at most one vertex. If a vertex rrr has two distinct outgoing neighbors that each guarantee delivery to ttt, then rrr guarantees delivery to ttt.

Proof. For every pursuer position c≠rc\ne rc=r, one of the two successors lies outside C(c)C(c)C(c). Move there. It survives every intervening pursuer response, after which its guaranteed strategy applies. If the chosen vertex is ttt, delivery is already terminal. This is a finite concatenation of actual strategies. □\square□

Balanced complementary halves

Lemma 17. For positive xxx, the xxx-subsets of [2x][2x][2x] can be partitioned into two coordinate-balanced families with complementary subsets in opposite families if and only if xxx is not a power of two.

High-girth complements and exact dense intervals

The preceding periodic construction attains the largest possible density of a noncomplete all-delivery network on an arithmetic progression. A different construction handles every sufficiently large order and an interval of arc counts. Here the sparse graph specifies the connections to omit from an otherwise complete directed network.

Lemma 18 (high-girth complement). Let FFF be an orientation of a finite simple undirected graph of girth at least six. Suppose every vertex has outdegree at least two in FFF. Let GGG contain exactly the nonloop arcs absent from FFF. Then every source–recipient pair in GGG is guaranteed within two messenger moves.

Proof. Diagonal and direct pairs need no argument. For a missing pair (s,t)(s,t)(s,t) of GGG, the arc s→ts\to ts→t belongs to FFF. Set B=NF+(s)∪NF−(t). B=N_F^+(s)\cup N_F^-(t). B=NF+​(s)∪NF−​(t). Both sss and ttt belong to BBB. In the underlying undirected graph, the vertices of BBB form an induced double star: its centers are s,ts,ts,t, the other outneighbors of sss are leaves at sss, and the other predecessors of ttt are leaves at ttt. The two sets of leaves are disjoint, since an overlap would make a triangle. An additional edge inside BBB would make a triangle or quadrilateral. Thus the distance between any two vertices in this induced tree is at most three.

Fix an initial pursuer vertex c≠sc\ne sc=s. If c∉Bc\notin Bc∈/B, two neighbors of ccc in BBB would form an undirected cycle of length at most five, so ccc has at most one outgoing FFF-neighbor in BBB. The same bound holds when c∈B∖{s}c\in B\setminus\{s\}c∈B∖{s}: a leaf at sss has its only incident edge in the tree directed toward it; a leaf at ttt has only its edge toward ttt; and all tree edges incident with ttt point into ttt.

Since ccc has at least two outgoing FFF-neighbors, choose u∈NF+(c)∖B.u\in N_F^+(c)\setminus B.u∈NF+​(c)∖B. Then u≠s,tu\ne s,tu=s,t, and s→us\to us→u and u→tu\to tu→t are arcs of GGG. Also u≠cu\ne cu=c and c→uc\to uc→u is absent from GGG. The messenger moves to uuu, survives every pursuer response, and delivers to ttt on its next turn. □\square□

The lemma only requires a lower bound on outgoing degrees. In particular, edges can later be added to the underlying graph and oriented arbitrarily, provided its girth remains at least six.

Theorem 19 (the densest noncomplete all-delivery networks). For every n≥52n\ge52n≥52, M(n,n(n−3))=2n.M(n,n(n-3))=2n.M(n,n(n−3))=2n. An attaining graph guarantees every pair within two messenger moves. The construction for n≥130n\ge130n≥130 has the ordinary proof below; the extension to 52≤n<13052\le n<13052≤n<130 uses an explicit finite structural certificate.

Proof. We first construct a four-regular undirected graph of girth at least six at each required order. Orient an Euler tour in each of its components. Every vertex then has two incoming and two outgoing arcs. Such tours exist by the elementary closed-trail construction: even degrees prevent an unused-edge trail from stopping away from its starting vertex, and further closed trails can be spliced into the first until all edges of the component have been used. Lemma 18 applies to the resulting orientation FFF. It has 2n2n2n arcs, so its directed complement has n(n−3)n(n-3)n(n−3) arcs and exactly 2n2n2n missing pairs, all guaranteed. The missing-pair count is also an upper bound for III.

For a building block, take point vertices p∈Z/13Zp\in\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Zp∈Z/13Z and line vertices ℓ∈Z/13Z\ell\in\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Zℓ∈Z/13Z, joining them when p−ℓ∈{0,1,3,9}.p-\ell\in\{0,1,3,9\}.p−ℓ∈{0,1,3,9}. This graph has 26 vertices and is four-regular. The twelve ordered differences between distinct members of {0,1,3,9}\{0,1,3,9\}{0,1,3,9} are precisely the twelve nonzero residues modulo 13. Consequently two distinct points cannot have two common line neighbors: the two common neighbors would give two representations of the same nonzero difference. There is no four-cycle. Bipartiteness excludes odd cycles, so the girth is at least six.

The following operation increases the order by one. Choose edges ababab and cdcdcd such that every endpoint of the second is at distance at least four from every endpoint of the first. Delete these two edges, add a new vertex xxx, and join xxx to a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d. The endpoints are distinct and all degrees remain four. Any new cycle uses two of these new edges. If their old endpoints belonged to the same removed edge, the path between them after its removal has length at least five, giving a new cycle of length at least seven. Otherwise their old distance was at least four, giving a new cycle of length at least six. Thus the operation preserves the required girth.

Such an edge pair exists in every four-regular graph with more than 120 vertices. Fix an edge ababab and let SSS consist of the vertices within distance three of aaa or bbb. The branching bound from the two ends of the edge gives ∣S∣≤2(1+3+9+27)=80.|S|\le2(1+3+9+27)=80.∣S∣≤2(1+3+9+27)=80. The induced graph on SSS is connected, hence has at least ∣S∣−1|S|-1∣S∣−1 edges. If there were no edge with both endpoints outside SSS, four-regularity would give 4∣V∖S∣=e(S,V∖S)=4∣S∣−2e(S)≤2∣S∣+2. 4|V\setminus S|=e(S,V\setminus S) =4|S|-2e(S) \le2|S|+2. 4∣V∖S∣=e(S,V∖S)=4∣S∣−2e(S)≤2∣S∣+2. It would follow that n≤⌊3∣S∣+12⌋≤120.n\le\left\lfloor\frac{3|S|+1}{2}\right\rfloor\le120.n≤⌊23∣S∣+1​⌋≤120. Therefore an outside edge exists and can serve as cdcdcd.

Start with five disjoint copies of the 26-vertex building block. Repeated insertion now gives every order n≥130n\ge130n≥130. For the smaller stated orders, two disjoint building blocks give order 52. The supplied certificate lists 78 admissible insertions, producing every order from 52 through 130. Each insertion satisfies the same distance condition and therefore has the proof of correctness just given. Its finite verification is described below. □\square□

The density n(n−3)n(n-3)n(n−3) is maximal among noncomplete all-delivery graphs, by the earlier dense-boundary theorem. This construction therefore settles the joint extremum at that density for every n≥52n\ge52n≥52; it is not a claim about the arc-only maximum at the same number of arcs.

Finite-certificate reproduction. The file research/extremal-bounds-girth-growth.json records the two removed edges at every insertion, starting from the explicit 52-vertex graph above. The generator and replayer src/extremal_bounds_girth_family.py checks the endpoint distances, all degrees, and the absence of short cycles. A separate implementation, src/extremal_bounds_girth_verify.py, rebuilds the incidence graph directly and checks girth by enumerating simple paths and testing whether they close into cycles of lengths three, four, or five. It verifies all 79 graph orders independently of the generator’s edge-deleted breadth-first checks. The receipt research/extremal-bounds-girth-verification.json records the certificate and verifier hashes. These are finite graph certificates attached to the proved insertion rule, not extrapolation from successful pursuit-game searches. They are executable checks rather than a Lean formalization; omitting this finite certificate leaves the ordinary theorem for every n≥130n\ge130n≥130.

Proof. Begin with the four-regular girth-six graph from Theorem 19. Repeatedly add an undirected edge between two vertices of current degree less than DDD whose distance is at least five. The final edge count is consequently at least D(n−∣U∣)+4∣U∣2≥Dn−(D−4)BD2. \frac{D(n-|U|)+4|U|}{2} \ge\frac{Dn-(D-4)B_D}{2}. 2D(n−∣U∣)+4∣U∣​≥2Dn−(D−4)BD​​. An infinite family attaining the sparse bounds

The five-type graph used in the dense construction also attains the sparse vertex and arc-budget bounds. This requires a different strategy: its messenger may need to travel around a substantial part of the ring. The proof combines fixed local certificates with a simulation valid at every sufficiently large circumference, followed by six finite base cases.

Theorem 21 (uniform sparse attainment). For every integer k≥4k\ge4k≥4, every source–recipient pair in HkH_kHk​ is guaranteed. Consequently MV(5k)=5k(5k−3),ME(10k)=5k(5k−3). M_V(5k)=5k(5k-3),\qquad M_E(10k)=5k(5k-3). MV​(5k)=5k(5k−3),ME​(10k)=5k(5k−3). For k≥10k\ge10k≥10, a sufficient delivery time is 8k+168k+168k+16 messenger moves. The theorem is computer-assisted: its finite ingredients are the two local objectives specified below and the six rings 4≤k≤94\le k\le94≤k≤9.

The stronger local arena

Unwrap the column coordinate to the integers, retaining the same two arc rules. Confine the messenger to columns −3,…,3-3,\ldots,3−3,…,3, disallowing moves out of this interval. Represent the pursuer by its exact vertex in columns −4,…,4-4,\ldots,4−4,…,4, together with an exterior state Ω\OmegaΩ. Thus there are 35 messenger positions and 46 pursuer positions.

Within its nine-column window the pursuer has all its usual moves and its wait; a move leaving the window goes to Ω\OmegaΩ. From Ω\OmegaΩ it may wait or enter any vertex of either boundary column −4-4−4 or 444. This grants more freedom than a particular physical pursuer outside the window. The messenger and Ω\OmegaΩ can never coincide.

The two objectives have different stopping rules:

  • A safe transfer ends in column zero at the start of a messenger turn, with the positions distinct. Entering column zero on a messenger move is insufficient: the intervening pursuer response must also be survived.
  • A delivery ends immediately when the messenger enters a specified vertex (0,t)(0,t)(0,t), before collision is checked there, exactly as in the original game.

For each objective, the certificate assigns nonnegative integer ranks to winning states and selects a legal move at every positive-rank messenger state. Every selected move decreases rank, and every legal response at a positive-rank pursuer state also decreases rank. The zero-rank states are precisely the applicable terminal successes. These conditions prove termination by induction on rank. For safe transfer, only noncollision messenger-turn states in column zero are seeded as successes; pursuer-turn states there still require all their responses to be safe.

The checked finite bounds are:

Safe transfer to column zero 1 225 8
Delivery to (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) 2 225 24
Delivery to (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) 2 225 16
Delivery to (0,2)(0,2)(0,2) 2 225 16
Delivery to (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) 2 225 17
Delivery to (0,4)(0,4)(0,4) 2 225 18

Each row covers all five source types and all 46 pursuer states other than the source itself. In particular, it includes an initially exterior pursuer. Only the bounds 8 and 24 are needed below; optimality of these local times is not claimed as a separate result.

Projection to a ring

Fix k≥10k\ge10k≥10 and any reference column. Its nine offsets −4,…,4-4,\ldots,4−4,…,4 represent distinct columns of the ring. Map a physical pursuer in this window to its exact local position and every other pursuer position to Ω\OmegaΩ.

Every physical pursuer move has a permitted image. A move within the window is unchanged, one leaving it goes to Ω\OmegaΩ, and a move remaining outside is represented by waiting at Ω\OmegaΩ. A move from outside into the window can enter only a boundary column, because each arc changes the column by at most one; every such entry is permitted from Ω\OmegaΩ. At k=10k=10k=10 the exterior consists of a single column adjacent to both boundaries, and both entries are already allowed. At k=9k=9k=9 the two boundary columns themselves have wraparound adjacencies, so this argument would fail; those rings are deliberately covered by finite checks instead.

Every messenger move permitted by the local certificate is a genuine ring move. Its seven represented columns lie strictly inside the pursuer window. Consequently a physical collision with the messenger is exactly a local collision; an exterior pursuer cannot coincide with it. Following a local winning strategy therefore succeeds against every physical pursuer strategy. This is a simulation of legal moves and collisions, not an assumption that winning strategies pass automatically to graph covers.

Composition and termination

Proof of Theorem 21. Translate the recipient’s column to zero, and let the messenger’s current column be ddd. Translate the safe-transfer window so that its local column zero is the physical column d−1d-1d−1; the messenger then starts in local column one. The certificate reduces its physical column by one modulo kkk and finishes only after the pursuer’s response, so another transfer can begin with the correct turn order. Recenter the window between transfers; each new local certificate is valid for every resulting noncollision pursuer position.

After the least nonnegative residue of d−2d-2d−2 modulo kkk such transfers, at most k−1k-1k−1, the messenger is in column two. Apply the delivery certificate for the recipient’s type. This takes at most 8(k−1)+24=8k+168(k-1)+24=8k+168(k−1)+24=8k+16 messenger moves. If a transfer encounters the actual recipient earlier, terminal receipt wins immediately and only shortens the play. Thus the argument guarantees finite delivery, not merely indefinite safe movement.

For 4≤k≤94\le k\le94≤k≤9, the explicit finite-ring certificates verify every source and pursuer position for each of the five recipient types in column zero. Translating columns gives every recipient. These six checks, together with the uniform argument for k≥10k\ge10k≥10, establish universality for all k≥4k\ge4k≥4.

Finally, a universal graph with n=5kn=5kn=5k vertices and 2n2n2n arcs has I(Hk)=n2−n−2n=n(n−3).I(H_k)=n^2-n-2n=n(n-3).I(Hk​)=n2−n−2n=n(n−3). The vertex upper bound and the even arc-budget upper bound both equal this number. Hence both asserted extremal equalities follow. □\square□

Certificate reproduction and scope. The file research/five-type-certificates.json contains the fixed local arena, ranks, and chosen messenger moves, generated and directly checked by src/five_type_certificate.py. The independent implementation src/five_type_local_verify.py constructs the explicit alternating-state graph from the arc rules and checks every winning rank condition, as well as closure of the losing region. Its full ranks and selected moves are saved in research/five-type-independent-local-certificates.json, together with the implementation hash. Both implementations agree on the six local bounds above. The six finite bases are stored in research/five-type-small-ring-certificates.json, including complete arc lists, messenger-move layers, and explicit alternating-state rank certificates for the five representative recipient types. The script src/five_type_small_certificates.py reproduces those checks using both game solvers and verifies every certificate transition. The ordinary projection and composition proof explains why these finite arrays certify infinitely many rings. This theorem is not currently claimed as a Lean formalization.

Proposition 24 (with a finite exhaustive computation). We have ME(7)=2. M_E(7)=2. ME​(7)=2.

Proof. First consider a weakly connected digraph with at most seven arcs and at least seven vertices. Forget the directions but retain one undirected edge for each arc, so that opposite arcs become parallel edges. The resulting connected multigraph has at most as many edges as vertices. It is therefore a tree or has exactly one cycle; a parallel pair is allowed as a cycle of length two.

In a tree, any reachable indirect source–recipient pair has an internal vertex separating its endpoints. A pursuer can start and wait there, preventing delivery. Thus no indirect pair is guaranteed. In the unicyclic case, a pair with either endpoint outside the unique cycle likewise has an internal separating vertex, unless its endpoints are adjacent in the underlying graph. For adjacent endpoints off the cycle, a directed route exists only if their connecting arc has the required direction, making the pair direct. Thus every counted pair must have both endpoints on the cycle.

There are exactly two simple undirected paths along that cycle between two distinct cycle vertices. If only one is a directed path from the source to the recipient, it is either a direct arc or has an internal vertex where the pursuer can wait. If neither is directed, the recipient is unreachable. Excursions into attached trees cannot bypass an internal cycle vertex. Consequently a counted pair requires both cycle paths to be directed from its source to its recipient. This forces the cycle’s unique divergence at that source and unique convergence at that recipient; every other cycle vertex has one entering and one leaving cycle edge. A fixed orientation can therefore support at most one such ordered pair. A cycle of length two consists of opposite arcs and supports no indirect pair. We have proved that every weakly connected digraph with at most seven arcs and at least seven vertices has I(G)≤1I(G)\le1I(G)≤1.

For a general digraph with seven arcs, distinct weak components contribute additively to I(G)I(G)I(G). Each component with a positive contribution uses at least four arcs by Proposition 23, so at most one component contributes. If that component uses at most six arcs, Proposition 23 bounds its contribution by two. If it uses seven arcs and has at least seven vertices, the preceding argument bounds its contribution by one. In the only remaining case it has at most six vertices. Adding isolated vertices to make six does not change its indirect guarantee count, and the complete six-vertex enumeration gives a maximum of two at seven arcs.

This last finite assertion is the computational dependency of the proposition. It is reproduced by src/enumerate_small_n6.cpp; the result is recorded with complete: true in research/solver-enumeration-n6.json. The enumeration covers every six-vertex digraph up to the degree-ordering reduction described in the computational section; the witness is also checked by the separate explicit-turn solver. The structural reduction above is what extends that finite calculation to unrestricted vertex counts.

Finally, add one disjoint arc to the six-arc, two-recipient construction in Proposition 23. This preserves its two guarantees and supplies seven arcs, proving the matching lower bound. □\square□

Attainment across densities and losses near completeness

Angel Raychev proposed that, for every sufficiently large nnn, the missing-pair bound should be attained at every integer budget 2n≤m≤n(n−3).2n\le m\le n(n-3).2n≤m≤n(n−3). The results in this section provide the probabilistic and dense ingredients of that proof. Raychev also proposed separating existence from explicit constructions and studying how domination destroys missing pairs as the graph approaches completeness. These distinctions motivate the statements below; their proofs were developed in the September 2026 follow-up investigation.

The underlying graph of FFF still has girth at least six. The new edges form a tree attached to the core at a,b,d,ea,b,d,ea,b,d,e, with ccc a pendant vertex. A new simple cycle with one segment in this tree has either a same-branch segment of length two and a core path of length at least four, or a cross-branch segment of length four and a core path of length at least two. A cycle with two tree segments must use the vertex-disjoint paths a−y−ba-y-ba−y−b and d−z−ed-z-ed−z−e: a cross-branch tree segment would meet any other segment. Its two core paths both join opposite branches and have length at least two, giving total length at least eight. With four attachment vertices there can be no third tree segment. Thus no cycle of length below six is introduced.

Every closed outgoing neighborhood in GGG is a subset of the corresponding translate of AAA. Distinct translates of AAA intersect in at most one point. This intersection property gives the following safe-branching rule. Fix a recipient. If two distinct outgoing neighbors of a vertex are already universally winning positions for that recipient, the vertex is universally winning as well. Against an initial cop at another vertex, at most one of the two successors lies in the cop’s closed outgoing neighborhood. Move to the other, survive the cop’s response, and use its winning strategy. The rule concerns the actual game, including the intervening pursuer move.

The proof is finite and constructive: initializing a quartet takes at most two messenger moves, and each quartet propagation increases a bound by at most four. The prime hypothesis is intentional. In an extension field, repeated addition only covers scalars from its prime subfield, so this four-move propagation does not justify the same conclusion for arbitrary prime powers. The five-type construction can tolerate a controlled set of additional arcs. The proof gives the pursuer every additional move while restricting the messenger to the original moves. This verifies all intermediate graphs at once, without assuming that winning is monotone under adding arcs.

It does not assert a practical numerical value of NNN or a short explicit construction at every budget in the latter part. Sparse endpoint attainment at every order from twelve

A second periodic construction admits controlled removal of vertices. Unlike a finite modification checked at one circumference, the removal is certified in a fixed local game that applies at every translated position. Separating the removals then provides all residue classes of the vertex count.

The removals inside the represented pursuer window form a subset of {−6,…,6}\{-6,\ldots,6\}{−6,…,6} with consecutive gaps at least three. There are exactly 189 such subsets. For every one of these patterns, the following finite local claims have complete rank certificates:

Objective Initial messenger column Maximum messenger moves

Each claim covers every existing initial messenger type and every noncolliding initial pursuer position, including Ω\OmegaΩ. We check that these local games represent every actual play on the ring. The thirteen pursuer columns are distinct and leave at least two exterior columns. Fix a recipient in column zero. Recenter and apply safe transfer repeatedly: each phase increases the messenger’s column by one and ends on an uncaught messenger turn, ready for the next phase. Bridging the entire sparse interval at every large order

The six-type construction can also support optional arcs. We keep those arcs away from deleted vertices, allowing two separately verified local strategies to cover every part of the graph.

With no deletions there are 8k≥n8k\ge n8k≥n. Thus any prescribed m−2n≤nm-2n\le nm−2n≤n of these arcs may be selected. It remains to prove that every such selection preserves universal delivery.

Consider local messenger columns [−4,4][-4,4][−4,4] and pursuer columns [−8,8][-8,8][−8,8], with an outside state Ω\OmegaΩ. The messenger uses only base arcs and may not leave its window. A pursuer move leaving its window enters Ω\OmegaΩ; from Ω\OmegaΩ it may wait or enter any existing vertex in columns −8,−7,−6,6,7,8-8,-7,-6,6,7,8−8,−7,−6,6,7,8. These three boundary layers cover every possible three-column re-entry.

There are two kinds of certified arenas:

  1. There is no deletion inside the pursuer window. The messenger has only the original six-type moves, while the pursuer has all eight optional arc types at every source column in its window.
  2. There is one deletion, at some offset h∈[−8,8]h\in[-8,8]h∈[−8,8]. Both players use the smoothed base moves; the pursuer still has the same three-layer outside re-entry rule.

The finite certificates prove safe transfer from any existing type in column −1-1−1 to column zero in at most nine messenger moves, and delivery from any existing type in column −2-2−2 to any existing recipient in column zero in at most 35 moves. The transfer completes only on a messenger turn after the pursuer response, with distinct positions. Delivery has immediate receipt priority. There are 125 certificates: seven for the augmented unmodified arena, and seven for each of the 17 possible deletion offsets, except for the absent recipient at (0,4)(0,4)(0,4) when h=0h=0h=0.

Every actual local window fits one of these cases. Its 17 represented pursuer columns have diameter 16, so cannot contain two deletions. If it contains a deletion hhh, each represented pursuer source column is at cyclic distance at most 16 from hhh, and hence none of its optional arcs was allowed. If it contains no deletion, the augmented arena contains every possible actual pursuer move and every messenger move used by the strategy. An exterior deletion changes no represented-to-represented base arc: the only affected boundary tail has both its original and smoothed heads outside. Discarded messenger exits are likewise unaffected.

All actual moves have column displacement at most three. Since k≥404k\ge404k≥404, the exterior gap between the two ends of the represented pursuer window has at least three columns. No single move can cross that entire gap between two represented vertices. An exterior return lands in one of the three allowed boundary layers. Thus mapping every exterior pursuer to Ω\OmegaΩ correctly includes all possible responses. The actual pursuer has no options beyond the relevant certified arena.

Repeatedly use safe transfer to advance the messenger by one column, ending each phase after the pursuer response. At most k−1k-1k−1 transfers place it two columns before the recipient. Apply the appropriate delivery certificate. The total is at most 9(k−1)+35=9k+26.9(k-1)+35=9k+26.9(k−1)+35=9k+26. This proves universal delivery for every selected subset of optional arcs. All n(n−1)−mn(n-1)-mn(n−1)−m missing pairs are consequently guaranteed. □\square□

Corollary 42 (the complete main interval at all sufficiently large orders). There is an absolute integer NNN such that, for every n≥Nn\ge Nn≥N and every integer 2n≤m≤n(n−3)2n\le m\le n(n-3)2n≤m≤n(n−3), M(n,m)=n(n−1)−m.\boxed{M(n,m)=n(n-1)-m.}M(n,m)=n(n−1)−m.​

Proof. Increase the threshold from Corollary 39, if necessary, to be at least 2419. Theorem 41 supplies every integer budget from 2n2n2n to 3n3n3n; Corollary 39 supplies every remaining budget through n(n−3)n(n-3)n(n−3). □\square□

This proves Raychev’s main-interval conjecture with a sufficiently-large order threshold. The threshold NNN is not claimed to be 2419: the latter is sufficient for Theorem 41 only, while the combined existence argument retains the asymptotic threshold from Corollaries 26 and 39. The construction is explicit in the intervals furnished by Theorems 38 and 41; the middle-density existence step is probabilistic. The result does not settle odd arc-only extrema, the exact small-order threshold, or all joint extrema below 2n2n2n.

Deterministically constructing the probabilistic examples

The probabilistic existence argument can be made algorithmic without changing its density range. We give the conditional counts explicitly, since conditioning on an exact arc budget destroys independence between different candidate intermediaries.

Together with the explicit sparse and high-girth constructions, this makes the full main-interval theorem constructive by a deterministic algorithm for every sufficiently large nnn. Use Theorems 38 and 41 in their sparse ranges, the algorithm above where Theorem 25 applies, and the high-girth complement construction in the final dense portion. The proofs of Corollaries 26, 39, and 42 show that these ranges overlap. The unknown moderate-order onset remains a separate issue; algorithmic construction does not lower that threshold automatically.

The sufficient threshold 180018001800 is not asserted optimal. The endpoint already holds at every n≥12n\ge12n≥12; the first sparse interval starts at 107510751075 and the dense bridge at 166166166. The odd endpoint and completion of its degree defect

The odd arc-budget equality theorem prescribes a particularly small defect: on n=k+1n=k+1n=k+1 vertices there is one vertex uuu of outdegree one, a different vertex vvv of indegree one, all other indicated degrees are two, and the arc u→vu\to vu→v is absent. The candidate extremal value is ME(2n−1)=(n−2)(n−3).M_E(2n-1)=(n-2)(n-3).ME​(2n−1)=(n−2)(n−3). The equality theorem reduces attainment to guaranteeing every missing pair whose source differs from uuu and whose recipient differs from vvv. It does not make arbitrary deletion from, or completion to, a two-regular graph preserve the relevant guarantees.

Two necessary structural properties

Lemma. Every odd-extremal graph with the preceding degree pattern is strongly connected. Moreover, for each vertex ccc, the graph with ccc deleted has a directed path from every s∉{u,c}s\notin\{u,c\}s∈/{u,c} to every t∉{v,c}t\notin\{v,c\}t∈/{v,c}.

Proof. Each such ordered pair with s≠ts\ne ts=t is either a direct arc or a guaranteed missing pair. Against a pursuer initially at ccc and waiting there, any successful delivery path avoids ccc internally. Since its endpoints differ from ccc, it gives the asserted path in the deleted graph.

To prove strong connectivity without deleting a vertex, all vertices different from uuu already reach all vertices different from vvv. The unique predecessor bbb of vvv is different from uuu, because u→vu\to vu→v is absent. Thus all vertices other than uuu reach vvv by first reaching bbb. The unique successor aaa of uuu differs from uuu, and uuu reaches every vertex by first going to aaa. □\square□

These are necessary conditions, not substitutes for the full game: the pursuer can move, so ordinary connectivity and stationary separators do not establish an attaining strategy.

Completing an odd extremizer can fail

Its completed indirect count is 276, whereas a universally winning two-regular graph on 19 vertices would have 304.

src/odd_endpoint_completion.py contains the fixed graph and runs both independent game solvers, checking every winning rank and every losing closure obligation. research/odd-endpoint-completion-certificate.json stores the complete finite certificates for the original and completed graphs. The ordinary trap proves nonuniversality without computation; the original graph’s attainment and the completed count 276 use the verified finite certificates. This example is not presently embedded in Lean. The subsequent construction settles the odd endpoint at every sufficiently large budget.

A useful degree-preserving search operation

Given a two-in/two-out graph, split one vertex www into vertices v,uv,uv,u. Assign one old incoming and one old outgoing arc to each new vertex, then add v→uv\to uv→u. This adds one vertex and one arc, giving exactly the odd equality degree pattern: vvv has indegree one and outdegree two, while uuu has indegree two and outdegree one. The forbidden opposite arc u→vu\to vu→v is absent because the original graph was loopless.

This operation supplies a structured family to investigate, but it is not a preservation theorem. A split of the 20-vertex five-type graph attains ME(41)=342M_E(41)=342ME​(41)=342, while all twenty canonical splits of its 30-vertex member fail to attain the corresponding odd bound. Likewise, changing the two horizontal lane speeds to three produces attaining single-arc deletions at 40 and 50 vertices but failures at neighboring and larger orders. These counterchecks prevent promoting isolated success to a uniform construction. A different six-type family supplies the following uniform positive result.

A proved infinite family attaining the odd bound

Construct a local arena with messenger columns [−4,4][-4,4][−4,4], pursuer columns [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6], and a pursuer outside state Ω\OmegaΩ. The messenger may use only moves remaining in its represented columns. The pursuer may leave to Ω\OmegaΩ, wait there, and re-enter at any vertex in columns −6,−5,5,6-6,-5,5,6−6,−5,5,6. Include both the unchanged arena and, for each h∈{−6,…,6}h\in\{-6,\ldots,6\}h∈{−6,…,6}, the arena with the translated arc (h,0)→(h,1)(h,0)\to(h,1)(h,0)→(h,1) deleted.

In every such arena the certificates prove two kinds of statement:

  • From each vertex of column −1-1−1 other than the degree-one source, reach some vertex of column zero other than that source safely, at the beginning of a messenger turn, in at most 14 moves.
  • From each vertex of column −2-2−2 other than the degree-one source, deliver to each recipient in column zero other than the degree-one recipient, in at most 26 moves.

All legal initial pursuer positions, including Ω\OmegaΩ, are quantified. Safe transfer goals exclude collision and are seeded only on messenger turns; delivery goals retain immediate terminal receipt. Two independent implementations check the full 97 objectives, all 44,850 required initial states, and every winning-rank and losing-closure condition. These are finite proof certificates for the displayed local statements.

For q≥15q\ge15q≥15, the thirteen pursuer columns are distinct and at least two columns remain outside. Every actual move changes its column by at most one, so an outside pursuer can first re-enter only at a permitted boundary column. No represented move can jump across the outside gap. The actual game therefore projects into this stronger local arena. A deletion in the represented columns gives one of the listed translated modules; otherwise the module is unchanged.

Fix an eligible recipient. Repeated safe transfers advance the messenger one column at a time until it reaches the column two places before the recipient. At most q−1q-1q−1 transfers are needed. Each transfer avoids the exceptional source even at its final state, so the next module’s initial requirement continues to hold. The delivery module then applies. This proves finite delivery in at most 14(q−1)+26=14q+1214(q-1)+26=14q+1214(q−1)+26=14q+12 moves.

Finally, there are (n−1)2(n-1)^2(n−1)2 pairs with an eligible source and recipient. Exactly n−2n-2n−2 are diagonal. The unique arc leaving uuu and the unique arc entering vvv are distinct because u→vu\to vu→v is absent, so precisely (2n−1)−2=2n−3(2n-1)-2=2n-3(2n−1)−2=2n−3 arcs belong to this rectangle. Hence the number of eligible missing pairs is (n−1)2−(n−2)−(2n−3)=(n−2)(n−3). (n-1)^2-(n-2)-(2n-3)=(n-2)(n-3). (n−1)2−(n−2)−(2n−3)=(n−2)(n−3). All are guaranteed, and the odd arc-budget upper bound proves equality. □\square□

We now specify the finite strategy lemmas and explain exactly how they apply to arbitrary qqq. Work first in the infinite column strip. In a local arena the messenger is restricted to columns [−5,5][-5,5][−5,5]; the pursuer has columns [−7,7][-7,7][−7,7] together with an outside state Ω\OmegaΩ. Inside these windows both players have their actual graph moves and may wait.   • Safe transfer: from column −d-d−d, reach a surviving vertex of column zero different from uuu, at the start of a messenger turn.
  • Delivery: from column −2d-2d−2d, deliver to any surviving recipient in column zero different from vvv.

In both statements the starting messenger vertex must differ from uuu. For r=5r=5r=5, where d=−1d=-1d=−1, safe transfer instead permits either column zero or column −1-1−1 as its final column, and delivery is guaranteed from either column 222 or column 333. The exclusion of uuu at the starting and final transfer states remains unchanged. Safe transfer goals exclude collision and are terminal only at the start of a messenger turn. Delivery goals give receipt priority over collision, exactly as in the original game.

The primary checker verifies all 903 local objectives with the same windows for all six rows. A separately written checker verifies the five nonempty deletion patterns in 750 objectives, covering 425,176 required initial states and 7,590,092 explicit alternating states. The unchanged-vertex pattern has its earlier independent 97-objective certificate. Every certificate includes the full attractor ranks and checks each existential messenger move and every universal pursuer response. Thus the displayed local statements are finite lemmas, not inferences from testing increasing ring lengths.

For the projection to a cyclic graph, represent the fifteen pursuer columns by their consecutive integer lifts. All actual moves have column jump at most two. An outside pursuer can therefore first enter only one of the four boundary columns allowed from Ω\OmegaΩ. Since q≥25q\ge25q≥25, the outside gap has at least ten columns, so no move can cross that gap between the two represented ends. Messenger positions remain in their eleven distinct represented columns, and Ω\OmegaΩ cannot conceal a collision there. Consequently each actual pursuer move has a permitted projected response in the stronger local arena.

The only defect anchors which can affect a represented outgoing move are within nine columns of the arena center, since changed tails lie within two columns of their anchor. Vertex deletions and the two degree exceptions are covered by the same bound. Testing anchors from −10-10−10 to 101010 therefore covers every relevant configuration. This interval has length 21, less than qqq, so at most one periodic copy of the defect can occur in it. If no copy occurs, the unchanged arena applies. These observations prove the projection for every cyclic position of the local window.

Fix a source other than uuu and a recipient other than vvv. For r≤4r\le4r≤4, repeatedly apply safe transfer in direction ddd until the messenger is two columns before the recipient. At most q−1q-1q−1 transfers are needed, after which the delivery module applies. Each transfer ends at a messenger turn away from uuu, so it satisfies its next module’s initial requirements regardless of the pursuer’s history.

In every case at most qqq transfers suffice. This proves finite delivery, uniformly bounded by 34q+2734q+2734q+27 moves.

Every missing pair with source different from uuu and recipient different from vvv is therefore guaranteed. Proof. Theorem 45 covers n≥145n\ge145n≥145. For every one of the remaining 132 integers 13≤n≤14413\le n\le14413≤n≤144, the supplementary data give a fixed simple graph with 2n−12n-12n−1 arcs, one outdegree-one vertex uuu, one different indegree-one vertex vvv, all other corresponding degrees two, and u→vu\to vu→v absent. The displayed six-type residue families supply most of these graphs. Deleting one arc from independently verified finite two-regular examples supplies the remaining orders from 19 upward. Six further fixed witnesses cover orders 13 through 18.

For every recipient other than vvv, the finite certificates specify an integer rank for every explicit messenger-turn and pursuer-turn state. Terminal receipt has rank zero, nonterminal collision has rank −1-1−1, and every other nonnegative messenger rank has a legal successor of smaller nonnegative rank. Every legal successor of a nonnegative pursuer rank has smaller nonnegative rank. The direct checker verifies these conditions against the original graph, together with the entire complementary losing closure. Every initial messenger state whose source differs from uuu and whose pursuer position differs from the source has nonnegative rank. Strict rank descent therefore forces finite delivery from each required state against every pursuer policy. This proves all required guarantees for each listed graph.

The full check contains 10,236 recipient objectives and 215,967,810 explicit alternating states. The same degree count as in Theorem 45 then gives (n−2)(n−3)(n-2)(n-3)(n−2)(n−3) guaranteed missing pairs. The arc-only upper bound applies to all support sizes, and hence also to the fixed support size nnn. This proves both equalities. □\square□

Proposition (small odd exceptions; exhaustive finite check). For 6≤k≤116\le k\le116≤k≤11, the general odd upper bound is not attained: ME(2k+1)≤k(k−3)+1.M_E(2k+1)\le k(k-3)+1.ME​(2k+1)≤k(k−3)+1. In particular, ME(23)≤89M_E(23)\le89ME​(23)≤89.

Proof. Equality in the upper bound k(k−3)+2k(k-3)+2k(k−3)+2 would, by the equality characterization, have precisely n=k+1n=k+1n=k+1 nonisolated vertices, one outdegree-one vertex uuu, one distinct indegree-one vertex vvv, all other corresponding degrees two, and u→vu\to vu→v absent. Add this missing arc. The resulting two-in/two-out digraph is a bipartite two-regular graph when its sources and recipients are represented in separate parts. Each of its bipartite cycles has even length, so alternating edge colors decompose it into two permutation factors A,BA,BA,B. Choose AAA to contain u→vu\to vu→v and label u=0,v=1u=0,v=1u=0,v=1.

Up to relabeling fixing these two vertices, the AAA-cycle through zero is (0,1,…,ℓ−1)(0,1,\ldots,\ell-1)(0,1,…,ℓ−1) for one ℓ≥2\ell\ge2ℓ≥2. Its other cycles are represented by an integer partition of n−ℓn-\elln−ℓ into parts at least two. For each such choice, enumerating all permutations BBB with B(i)≠i,A(i)B(i)\ne i,A(i)B(i)=i,A(i) covers every candidate graph; remove 0→10\to10→1 before applying any game test.

Two necessary obstructions safely prune this enumeration. Once the outgoing neighborhood of an eligible source sss is complete, if some c≠sc\ne sc=s has N+(s)⊆N+[c]N^+(s)\subseteq N^+[c]N+(s)⊆N+[c] and there is an eligible missing recipient for sss, the pursuer can wait at ccc and capture the first nonwaiting messenger move. Once the incoming neighborhood of an eligible recipient ttt is complete, if N−(t)⊆N+[c]N^-(t)\subseteq N^+[c]N−(t)⊆N+[c] and there is an eligible source outside N−(t)∪{t,c}N^-(t)\cup\{t,c\}N−(t)∪{t,c}, waiting at ccc until the messenger first enters N−(t)N^-(t)N−(t) likewise permits capture. In a partial assignment the cop’s outgoing row may be incomplete: coverage already present persists under later additions. The source or recipient neighborhood used in the inclusion is always complete. The code checks explicitly that the required eligible missing partner exists.

All remaining completed graphs are evaluated by the exact finite reachability game, with receipt priority and finite termination. Enumeration finishes at every 7≤n≤127\le n\le127≤n≤12 and finds no attaining graph. Its counts are:

Lemma (first reduction at 23 arcs). Every graph with 23 arcs satisfies I(G)≤87I(G)\le87I(G)≤87.

Proof. Write A,B,q,r,b,eA,B,q,r,b,eA,B,q,r,b,e as in the general arc-bound proof. Then q,r≤11q,r\le11q,r≤11, e≥2q+2r−23e\ge2q+2r-23e≥2q+2r−23, and I≤qr−b−eI\le qr-b-eI≤qr−b−e. We first show that I≥88I\ge88I≥88 would force one of three degree patterns on 12 nonisolated vertices.

If q,r≤10q,r\le10q,r≤10 the elementary bound is at most 83; if either is at most 9 it is at most 82. For (q,r)=(10,11)(q,r)=(10,11)(q,r)=(10,11), the bound is 91−b91-b91−b, so only b≤3b\le3b≤3 needs consideration. There are then at least six indegree-zero vertices in A∖BA\setminus BA∖B: all indegree outside BBB totals at most one. They emit at least twelve arcs. At most one recipient in BBB can have indegree three, and then no arc ends outside BBB; alternatively at most one arc ends outside BBB. At least nine of the twelve arcs therefore enter indegree-two recipients in BBB, producing at least five zero-contribution columns. This gives I≤10(11−5)=60I\le10(11-5)=60I≤10(11−5)=60. The case (11,10)(11,10)(11,10) uses the corresponding zero-row argument. Hence q=r=11q=r=11q=r=11.

If b≤7b\le7b≤7, at least three members of A∖BA\setminus BA∖B have indegree zero. Their at least six outgoing arcs produce at least two indegree-two zero columns by the same argument. Deleting those columns removes at most four of the at least 21 direct pairs, so I≤99−17=82I\le99-17=82I≤99−17=82. If b=8b=8b=8 or 9, there is at least one such zero column. Indeed, the two distinct successors of any indegree-zero member cannot both avoid indegree-two vertices of BBB: an indegree-three recipient already uses the whole available unit of indegree surplus. Removing the column gives I≤110−19−(b−1)=92−b≤84I\le110-19-(b-1)=92-b\le84I≤110−19−(b−1)=92−b≤84.

Suppose b=10b=10b=10, and write A∖B={v}A\setminus B=\{v\}A∖B={v}, B∖A={u}B\setminus A=\{u\}B∖A={u}. If vvv has indegree zero or uuu has outdegree zero, a zero column or row gives I≤82I\le82I≤82. Otherwise their respective degrees equal one and exhaust all indegree outside BBB and all outdegree outside AAA. All degrees in AAA and BBB equal two, and all other vertices are isolated. This gives the first two patterns below, according as u→vu\to vu→v is absent or present.

Finally suppose b=11b=11b=11, so A=B=CA=B=CA=B=C has 11 vertices. At most one arc starts outside CCC and at most one ends outside CCC. If all arcs lie in CCC, there are only 110−23=87110-23=87110−23=87 missing pairs. An arc with both endpoints outside CCC leaves a two-regular 11-vertex core; such a core is not universal by the completed small regular exclusion, so again I≤87I\le87I≤87. If there is exactly one crossing arc, either deleting it leaves a two-regular core, or its active endpoint has degree two and a zero-degree external neighbor. In the former case a losing core strategy still applies: the messenger cannot use an inaccessible external source or enter an external sink on a successful route to an eligible recipient. In the latter case an entire eligible row or column, containing at least nine missing pairs, contributes zero. Neither permits I≥88I\ge88I≥88.

If there are two crossing arcs, they are C→xC\to xC→x and y→Cy\to Cy→C. When x≠yx\ne yx=y, the same sink or indegree-zero-source obstruction applies. When x=yx=yx=y, this is the third pattern. Thus the only possibilities under I≥88I\ge88I≥88 are:

Pattern on 12 vertices Eligible missing pairs
Distinct degree-one source uuu and recipient vvv, all other corresponding degrees two, u→vu\to vu→v absent 90
The same distinct exceptions, with u→vu\to vu→v present 89
One vertex of both indegree and outdegree one, every other vertex two-in/two-out 89

All three finite classes can be covered by permutation factorization. For the first, add the missing 0→10\to10→1 as before. For the second, add a second copy of 0→10\to10→1 and factor the resulting bipartite multigraph; both permutation factors then contain 0→10\to10→1. For the third, add the dummy loop 0→00\to00→0 and choose the first factor to contain it. All other cycles of that factor have length at least two. Remove the added copy or loop before all game tests. These conventions cover every simple graph in the displayed classes.

The same camping prunes remain sound even for a search allowing a few failed pairs: a source obstruction destroys at least eight eligible missing pairs, and a recipient obstruction destroys at least seven. Since each class has at most 90 eligible missing pairs, no such graph can have I≥87I\ge87I≥87. For every surviving complete graph, the exact game now counts unsuccessful eligible source-recipient pairs; evaluation may stop only once the remaining possible count falls below 87.

All three enumerations complete and find no graph with I≥87I\ge87I≥87. The respective numbers of complete graphs surviving local obstructions are 16,902,091, 1,125,588, and 3,558,672. In particular none reaches 88, contradicting the proposed I≥88I\ge88I≥88. Therefore I(G)≤87I(G)\le87I(G)≤87. □\square□

Lemma (eleven-vertex cores). Every graph on 11 vertices with 22 or 23 arcs satisfies I(G)≤81I(G)\le81I(G)≤81.

Proof. A vertex of outdegree at most one leaves at most ten contributing source rows, each of size at most eight, giving I≤80I\le80I≤80. A low-indegree vertex gives the same column bound. We may therefore assume minimum indegree and outdegree two. At 22 arcs all degrees equal two. At 23 arcs exactly one vertex has outdegree three and exactly one has indegree three.

If a source camping obstruction occurs, at least eight missing pairs fail at 22 arcs, and at least seven fail at 23 arcs. If a recipient camping obstruction occurs at ttt with pursuer position ccc, every source outside N−(t)∪{t,c}N^-(t)\cup\{t,c\}N−(t)∪{t,c} fails. This gives at least seven failed pairs at 22 arcs and at least six at 23 arcs. The total numbers of missing pairs are 88 and 87, respectively, so every graph with one of these obstructions has I≤81I\le81I≤81.

It remains to enumerate the graphs with neither obstruction. The 22-arc case uses the two-permutation decomposition already described. For 23 arcs, the bipartite graph still has a perfect matching: a set SSS of source vertices emits at least 2∣S∣2|S|2∣S∣ edges, whereas a set of possible heads TTT can receive at most 2∣T∣+12|T|+12∣T∣+1. Thus ∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣|N(S)|\ge|S|∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣, which implies a perfect matching by the augmenting-path criterion. Its removal leaves residual degree one at every source except the unique degree-three source, where two choices remain; recipient capacities are analogous.

Fix the matching permutation to each cycle partition with no singleton. Its cycle rotations and permutations of equal-length cycles allow the degree-three source to be placed at one representative vertex for each distinct cycle length. Enumerate all positions of the degree-three recipient, then every residual row subject to the prescribed column capacities. This covers every graph in question. Only complete source rows or recipient columns are used in camping prunes; a partial cop row suffices because any coverage already present persists under later additions.

The complete 22-arc enumeration has 120,302 graphs surviving these prunes, with maximum I=66I=66I=66. The complete 23-arc enumeration has 792,080 such graphs, with maximum I=74I=74I=74. Both use the exact finite game recurrence and were freshly recompiled and replayed with all counts and witnesses matching. Thus the graphs surviving the prunes also have I≤81I\le81I≤81, proving the lemma. □\square□

Seven-vertex upper bound. If a graph has at most thirteen arcs, the arc-only bounds give I≤20I\le20I≤20; it suffices here to use monotonicity of MEM_EME​ (pad by disjoint one-way arcs) and ME(13)≤20M_E(13)\le20ME​(13)≤20. We describe the finite reduction and every rejection rule. Write Os=N+(s)O_s=N^+(s)Os​=N+(s), Pt=N−(t)P_t=N^-(t)Pt​=N−(t) and Cc={c}∪N+(c)C_c=\{c\}\cup N^+(c)Cc​={c}∪N+(c). A counted pair (s,t)(s,t)(s,t) necessarily satisfies

  2. Os⊈CcO_s\not\subseteq C_cOs​⊆Cc​ for every c≠sc\ne sc=s;
  3. Pt⊈CcP_t\not\subseteq C_cPt​⊆Cc​ for every c≠sc\ne sc=s.

The degree conditions are the one-neighbor camping obstructions. For condition 2, a pursuer waiting at ccc captures the messenger after its first departure from sss. For condition 3, it waits at ccc and captures the messenger upon the first entry into a predecessor of ttt, before the next messenger move can deliver. Indefinite waiting by the messenger also fails to deliver. These arguments respect receipt priority because an indirect source is not itself a predecessor of its recipient.

Let U(G)U(G)U(G) be the number of pairs satisfying these three conditions. Then I(G)≤U(G)I(G)\le U(G)I(G)≤U(G). A source contributes at most four pairs, so I≥22I\ge22I≥22 requires at least six sources of outdegree at least two. Every graph can be relabeled in nondecreasing outdegree order, allowing only the first row to have degree below two. We enumerate every loopless outgoing row mask in that order, with total degree between fourteen and twenty. This includes every possible graph, with harmless repetitions. At a partial assignment, the following bounds allow safe pruning:

  • A completed row of degree d≥2d\ge2d≥2 contributes at most 6−d6-d6−d, or zero if a known completed row already violates condition 2. Each remaining row contributes at most 6−max⁡(2,d0)6-\max(2,d_0)6−max(2,d0​), where d0d_0d0​ is the smallest outdegree still allowed by the ordering.
  • A target currently of indegree ddd contributes at most 6−max⁡(2,d)6-\max(2,d)6−max(2,d). Its contribution is zero if the remaining rows cannot raise its indegree to two.
  • The total arc count must remain extendible to the interval [14,20][14,20][14,20].

No omitted edge can repair a rejected completed source: the covering closed neighborhood only grows. The incoming-degree bounds likewise use upper estimates on all possible completions. At every surviving complete graph we count U(G)U(G)U(G) directly. The exhaustive enumeration has 109,941,961109,941,961109,941,961 recursion nodes and 4,299,6244,299,6244,299,624 complete leaves before an optional indegree tie normalization. None has U(G)≥22U(G)\ge22U(G)≥22. A separate implementation uses boolean adjacency, descending outdegree order, and no indegree tie normalization; it completes 123,280,819123,280,819123,280,819 nodes and the same 4,299,6244,299,6244,299,624 leaves, again with no survivor. This proves I≤21I\le21I≤21 in the remaining arc range. The lower witness proves equality.

Eight-vertex upper bound. At most fifteen arcs give I≤ME(15)≤30I\le M_E(15)\le30I≤ME​(15)≤30; at least twenty-four arcs leave at most thirty-two missing pairs. To exclude I≥33I\ge33I≥33, it therefore suffices to examine 16≤m≤2316\le m\le2316≤m≤23. Each source contributes at most five pairs, so at least seven sources must have outdegree at least two. The same camping conditions and partial bounds used above apply with eight vertices.

For this slightly larger search we also remove labeling redundancy. Fix a nondecreasing outdegree sequence. After the outgoing rows numbered less than rrr have been chosen, partition the unassigned vertices into cells with equal prescribed outdegree and identical adjacency from all completed rows. Vertices in such a cell may be permuted without changing any completed row or degree requirement. Therefore, when choosing row rrr, its neighbors among the future vertices of each cell may be required to form a prefix of that cell. This loses no graph: permute within each cell to put the neighbors first, fixing row rrr and all previous vertices, and continue recursively. The new cells are obtained by splitting the old cells, so their contiguity is preserved. The analogous suffix rule and reversed degree order are equally complete.

The primary search completes all 178178178 degree sequences, with 946,676,955946,676,955946,676,955 recursion nodes and 22,465,45322,465,45322,465,453 complete leaves. Only 373373373 leaves satisfy the necessary pair bound U(G)≥33U(G)\ge33U(G)≥33. Exact least-attractor evaluation rejects all of them; the largest actual III among these survivors is seventeen. Thus no graph has I≥33I\ge33I≥33, proving MV(8)=32M_V(8)=32MV​(8)=32. The ordinary canonicalization and every pruning rule were independently audited; as an additional small positive check, every labeled loopless four-vertex graph was canonicalized in both prefix and suffix conventions and its relabeling and prefix conditions checked. Independent complete suffix enumeration and the explicit alternating-state game provide a second finite verification: its completed intervals [0,160)[0,160)[0,160) and [160,178)[160,178)[160,178) cover all degree profiles. They visit 1,179,975,7701,179,975,7701,179,975,770 nodes and 63,717,03463,717,03463,717,034 complete leaves, with 1,1151,1151,115 static survivors, all rejected. The differing counts reflect the opposite degree order and suffix convention, which choose a different redundant collection of representatives. Both implementations give the same zero-survivor conclusion.

Nonattainment at orders eight through eleven. By the vertex equality criterion, an attaining graph would be universally winning and have indegree and outdegree exactly two everywhere. Any such directed graph is the union of two arc-disjoint permutation factors. Indeed, its bipartite tail/head incidence graph is two-regular, so alternating the edges around each even cycle gives the two perfect matchings. Both permutations are fixed-point-free. Up to simultaneous relabeling, the first permutation may be put in canonical cycle form for each partition of nnn having no part one; enumerate every second permutation avoiding both the diagonal and the first permutation’s arcs.

The source and predecessor camping conditions above reject a branch as soon as a completed two-element neighborhood is covered by a known closed outgoing neighborhood. For the predecessor condition, at least n−3≥2n-3\ge2n−3≥2 sources are indirect, so a covering vertex can be avoided as the initial source. Every remaining complete graph is evaluated by the finite least-attractor algorithm. The exhaustive counts are:

nnn Cycle partitions Recursion nodes Locally admissible complete graphs Universally winning graphs
7 4 142 0 0
8 7 1,446 0 0
9 8 10,996 535 0
10 12 231,676 35,610 0
11 14 2,177,946 120,302 0

An independent implementation reverses the permutation assignment order. Its local tests forbid directed transitive triangles, two distinct length-two walks with the same ordered endpoints, and duplicate completed outgoing pairs; these are precisely the same camping obstructions in adjacency-matrix form. It then uses an explicit alternating-state AND/OR queue attractor instead of the primary synchronous bitmask iteration. Both complete enumerations give exactly the displayed counts. As a positive control, a known universal twelve-vertex graph passes every incremental pruning test and the game check of the primary enumeration. Hence equality MV(n)=n(n−3)M_V(n)=n(n-3)MV​(n)=n(n−3) is impossible at these orders, which lowers the integer upper bound by one. □\square□

The seven-vertex example also gives the first noncomplete universally winning graph. At orders at most three, the previously established zero maximum excludes any missing guaranteed pair. At orders four through six, the density bound for a noncomplete universal graph would require m≤n(n−3)m\le n(n-3)m≤n(n−3) and hence I≥2nI\ge2nI≥2n, contradicting the exact maxima 2,4,72,4,72,4,7.

Verification boundary. These are finite computer-assisted proofs, with ordinary completeness and pruning arguments; they are not presently Lean formalizations. The negative seven-vertex result needs no game solver after the static camping reduction. The lower witnesses have saved rank certificates checked directly. Every remaining degree-two graph and every eight-vertex static survivor is evaluated by the exact game algorithms in the independent exhaustive runs; full per-graph ranks for those negative enumerations are not stored. The exact values at orders nine through eleven remain open; absence of a two-regular universal graph does not determine their extrema.

The combined joint maximum

The sparse constructions can be placed inside a larger network by adding isolated vertices. This observation joins the arc-budget extrema to the two dense regimes and gives a single eventual formula.

Proof. For even m=2k≥24m=2k\ge24m=2k≥24, Theorem 40 constructs an attaining kkk-vertex graph. If k≤nk\le nk≤n, add n−kn-kn−k isolated vertices. This does not change III: pairs between components have no delivery path; a pursuer starting at an added isolate stays there and cannot obstruct an existing delivery strategy. The arc-only upper bound supplies the matching upper bound for the joint problem.

For odd m=2k+1≥25m=2k+1\ge25m=2k+1≥25, Corollary 45.1 constructs an attaining graph on k+1=(m+1)/2k+1=(m+1)/2k+1=(m+1)/2 vertices. When m<2nm<2nm<2n, its support has at most nnn vertices. Add isolates and apply the odd arc-only upper bound. This gives k(k−3)+2k(k-3)+2k(k−3)+2.

Theorem 44 supplies the third case. Corollary 33 supplies the fourth, since its threshold 757575 is far below the present hypothesis. Finally Theorem 13 gives zero above n(n−2)n(n-2)n(n−2). The ranges cover every stated integer budget. □\square□

This is a complete joint classification in the displayed eventual range, with deterministic attaining constructions. It does not assert the same onset for smaller host orders, or fill the remaining finite odd and very small even arc budgets. In particular, the assertion that the full extremal problem is settled for every finite pair (n,m)(n,m)(n,m) would be stronger than what has been proved here.

A quadratic dense interval from three safe intermediaries

The sparse missing graph need not retain large girth while its density increases. Three designated outgoing missing arcs per vertex suffice, provided certain differences between their endpoints stay protected. The resulting construction covers a quadratic interval of missing-arc counts by a direct modular rule.

Exact arc maxima from eight through eleven

The six-vertex table supplies useful lower bounds, but does not itself settle an arc budget when the number of vertices is unrestricted. At eleven arcs the distinction is essential: seven vertices attain eight guarantees, exceeding the six-vertex maximum of seven.

Proof of the support reduction. Indirect guarantees add over weak components. Every component with a positive contribution has at least four arcs. At these budgets there can be at most two positive components. If there are two, each has at most seven arcs; Propositions 23 and 24 give a combined maximum of at most three. This cannot improve any of the displayed lower bounds.

There is therefore only one relevant positive component. We argue in increasing order of the budget m=8,9,10,11m=8,9,10,11m=8,9,10,11. If it uses all mmm arcs and has at least mmm vertices, the tree-or-unicyclic argument in Proposition 24 gives at most one indirect guarantee. That argument only needs a connected underlying multigraph with at most as many edges as vertices, so applies unchanged at the present budgets.

In the remaining case the component has at most m−1m-1m−1 vertices. Pad it with isolates to exactly m−1m-1m−1 vertices; its arc count and indirect count do not change. Hence each upper bound reduces to the following one finite counterexample test:

Proof. First construct a bipartite graph JpJ_pJp​ for each of the primes p=5,7p=5,7p=5,7. One part consists of the one-dimensional subspaces of Fp3\mathbb F_p^3Fp3​ and the other of its two-dimensional subspaces; join them when one is contained in the other. Equivalently, represent a point by a nonzero vector vvv up to nonzero scaling, a line by a nonzero linear form aaa up to scaling, and test a⋅v=0a\cdot v=0a⋅v=0. Two distinct points span a unique two-dimensional subspace. Thus two points cannot share two line neighbors, excluding four-cycles. Bipartiteness excludes odd cycles, so JpJ_pJp​ has girth at least six. In particular, J5J_5J5​ has 626262 vertices and degree six, while J7J_7J7​ has 114114114 vertices and degree eight.

Orient each remaining edge arbitrarily. Taking any subset of those additional arcs preserves minimum outgoing degree two and girth at least six in the underlying graph.

A local deletion set H⊆[−8,8]H\subseteq[-8,8]H⊆[−8,8] has at most five members and consecutive gaps at least three. For the moment omit all optional arcs from this arena.

Put H0=H∩[−6,6]H_0=H\cap[-6,6]H0​=H∩[−6,6] and consider the previously certified arena of Theorem 40 with these deletions, messenger columns [−4,4][-4,4][−4,4], pursuer columns [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6], and outside re-entry into columns ±5,±6\pm5,\pm6±5,±6. Keep every messenger position and every pursuer position in [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6], and map all remaining pursuer positions to the smaller arena’s Ω\OmegaΩ. This map includes every legal move of the larger arena:

  • The messenger moves coincide. A deletion outside [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6] affects no messenger tail or retained messenger destination.
  • A pursuer move with both endpoints in [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6] is unchanged. An exterior deletion can alter a represented tail only for h=7h=7h=7, changing 16→471_6\to4_716​→47​ into 16→281_6\to2_816​→28​; both heads map to Ω\OmegaΩ.
  • A pursuer outside [−6,6][-6,6][−6,6] moves at most two columns in the base graph. Any entry therefore lands in ±5\pm5±5 or ±6\pm6±6, where the smaller arena already permits arbitrary re-entry. The larger arena’s own outside transitions map either to Ω\OmegaΩ or to column ±6\pm6±6, also permitted.

The map preserves collisions because every messenger lies in [−4,4][-4,4][−4,4]. It preserves terminal receipt and the messenger-turn stopping condition for safe transfer. The old strategies therefore lift to the larger arena. They safely transfer any existing messenger in column −1-1−1 to column zero within nine moves, and deliver from column −2-2−2 to any existing recipient in column zero within 27 moves.

For a window with no deletion, instead use the fully augmented arena from Theorem 41, with the same radii and three re-entry layers. Its certificates give transfer within nine moves and delivery within 35. The messenger strategies use only base arcs; the optional arcs are included only among the pursuer’s possible responses. Thus removing any subset of the optional arcs leaves these strategies valid. Every actual window fits one of these two cases. If it contains a deletion, all its represented source columns have distance at most 16 from that deletion, so none of their optional arcs is present. If it contains no deletion, the fully augmented arena includes all actual pursuer moves. A deletion just outside the window changes no represented-to-represented base arc: at the right boundary, both the original and the smoothed head lie outside; at the left boundary the affected tail lies outside.

All actual moves have column displacement at most three. Since k≥180k\ge180k≥180, no move can cross the exterior gap between the represented ends and land back inside. Every exterior return lands in one of the three permitted boundary layers. Mapping an actual exterior pursuer to Ω\OmegaΩ therefore remains a valid simulation even if optional arcs occur outside the current window.

At most k−1k-1k−1 safe transfers move the messenger to the column two steps before its recipient. Each transfer ends on a messenger turn after the pursuer response, with distinct positions. The final delivery then takes at most 35 moves. The total bound is 9(k−1)+35=9k+26.9(k-1)+35=9k+26.9(k−1)+35=9k+26. All missing pairs are guaranteed, giving the stated equality. □\square□

Start with X0(t)=VX_0(t)=VX0​(t)=V and X0(r)=∅X_0(r)=\varnothingX0​(r)=∅ otherwise. The recurrence includes waits and excludes all nonterminal collisions. Its least fixed point enforces eventual delivery. A separate implementation builds the explicit alternating graph of states (r,c,turn)(r,c,\text{turn})(r,c,turn) and computes its reachability attractor. This is standard finite reachability-game machinery (Berwanger 2009), rather than a new general algorithm for graph games.

The certificate checker independently verifies decreasing ranks on the selected messenger moves and on every pursuer response. Outside the winning region it verifies closure under every messenger move and at least one pursuer response. Thus a negative answer comes with an avoidance strategy, not simply failure of a search. Standard adjacency-list attractor analysis gives an all-recipient time bound O(n2m+n3)O(n^2m+n^3)O(n2m+n3); that bound describes the standard implementation, not a claimed running-time bound for the simpler synchronous reference solver.
